q-94453.problem: A data set has mean $\overset{―}{x}=17$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=4.06.$ Find the $z$-score of an observation $x=12.3,$ giving your answer to $2$ decimal places.
q-94453.worked_solution:
The $z$-score of an observation $x$ is defined by

$$
z=\frac{x-\overset{―}{x}}{\sigma }.
$$

The $z$-score represents how many standard deviations an observation is above or below the data set's mean.

Here, we're told that the mean is $\overset{―}{x}=17,$ and we can calculate the standard deviation as

$$
\sigma =\sqrt{{\sigma }^{2}}=\sqrt{4.06}.
$$

So, the $z$-score of the observation $x=12.3$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{x-\overset{―}{x}}{\sigma } \\  & ≈\frac{12.3-17}{\sqrt{4.06}} \\  & ≈-2.33\end{aligned}
$$

to $2$ decimal places.

The point $P(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3},\frac{2}{3})$ lies on the unit circle, as shown. What is $\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ?$
q-64985.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14238118/assets/7895e1fbe54cd3dea65ba1c75d79c6f325f14cd6bc55f9c7ad99299f00b516df.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $x=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}$ and $y=\frac{2}{3}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Knowing that $\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ we can calculate $\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta :$

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =\frac{(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3})}{(\frac{2}{3})}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}.
$$

q-113727.name: Question 3
q-113727.worked_solution:
Let $u=2-{x}^{6}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-6{x}^{5}\,⟹\,(-\frac{1}{6})\text{d}u={x}^{5}\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{5}}{\sqrt{2-{x}^{6}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{2-{x}^{6}}}\cdot {x}^{5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-\frac{1}{6})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}(2\sqrt{u})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{u}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{2-{x}^{6}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-123853.name: Question 4
q-123853.problem:
Let $R=[5,6]\times [1,3]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)$ be a function defined over $R.$
The lower and upper Riemann sums corresponding to an arbitrary partition $P$ of $R$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(2{x}_{i-1}-3{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}, \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j-1})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the definition of the double integral in terms of $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P),$ compute ${∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:*

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}=({x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2})({y}_{n}-{y}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$
q-123853.worked_solution:
For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

First, notice that ${\overset{¯}{x}}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})$ will always lie between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$, and similarly ${\overset{¯}{y}}_{j}=\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})$ will always lie between ${y}_{j-1}$ and ${y}_{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
2{x}_{i-1}-3{y}_{j}\le 2\cdot \frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-3\cdot \frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j-1}
$$

which simplifies to

$$
2{x}_{i-1}-3{y}_{j}\le ({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{3}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j-1}.
$$

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{3}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})]Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P)
$$

Separating the sums using the addition and constant multiple rules, we get

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}-\frac{3}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P).
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =({6}^{2}-{5}^{2})(3-1)=22 \\ \frac{3}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{3}{2}({3}^{2}-{1}^{2})(6-5)=12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le 22-12\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le 10\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=10.
$$

q-36290.name: Question 5
q-36290.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}y$ at the point $A(1,0)$ in the direction towards the point $B(0,1).$
q-36290.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨0,1⟩-⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}}⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}y),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}y)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{y}+2xy,\,x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇\,f(1,0) & =⟨{e}^{0}+2\cdot 1\cdot 0,\,1\cdot {e}^{0}+{1}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,0) & =∇f(1,0)\cdot u \\  & =⟨1,\,2⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

q-143441.problem: If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ drawn from a population with mean $\mu =4$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=9,$  determine the smallest sample size required so that the standard error of the mean is less than $0.3.$
q-143441.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population variance ${\sigma }^{2},$ then

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}
$$

Since the population standard deviation is $\sigma =\sqrt{9}=3,$ we have that 

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{3}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We require that the standard error is less than $0.3.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{n}} & <0.3 \\ \sqrt{n} & >\frac{3}{0.3} \\ \sqrt{n} & >10 \\ n & >{10}^{2} \\ n & >100.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the smallest sample size is $n=101.$

q-99055.name: Question 8
q-99055.problem: What are the critical points of the function $f(x)=\frac{x-3}{{x}^{2}-5}?$
q-99055.worked_solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{x-3}{{x}^{2}-5}) \\  & =\frac{(x-3)^{′}\cdot ({x}^{2}-5)-(x-3)\cdot ({x}^{2}-5)^{′}}{({x}^{2}-5)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}-5)-(x-3)\cdot 2x}{({x}^{2}-5)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-5+6x-{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}-5)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{2}-6x+5}{({x}^{2}-5)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x$ by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{{x}^{2}-6x+5}{({x}^{2}-5)^{2}} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-6x+5 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+5 & =0 \\ (x-3)^{2}-9+5 & =0 \\ (x-3)^{2}-4 & =0 \\ (x-3)^{2} & =4 \\ x-3 & =\pm 2 \\ x & =1,\,5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=1$ and $x=5.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist at $x=\pm \sqrt{5}.$ But these points do not lie in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=1$ and $x=5.$

q-138856.name: Question 10
q-138856.problem:
Consider the function $y=(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{5x}.$ Its derivative is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=5(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{5x}\cdot g(x).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$
q-138856.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{5x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{5x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =5x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(5x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x))+(5x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =5\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+5x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-5x\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =5(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(5(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{5x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{5x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$

q-181650.name: Question 12
q-181650.problem:
Which of the following sets are infinite?

I. $A=\{{f}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}\}$

II. $B=\{{g}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}\}$

III. $C=\{{h}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}\}$
q-181650.worked_solution:
The cardinality of a finite set is the number of elements contained within it. A set is infinite if it has infinitely many elements.

- The set $A$ is infinite. Listing the first few elements of our set, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{(0)}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\ {f}^{(1)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\ {f}^{(2)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\ {f}^{(3)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)=8\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\ ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we can write our set as follows:

$$
A=\{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x,-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2x,8\operatorname{sin}⁡2x,…\}
$$

Consequently, $A$ is infinite.

- The set $B$ is finite. Listing the first few elements of our set, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{(0)}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {g}^{(1)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {g}^{(2)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {g}^{(3)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {g}^{(4)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $B$ contains four elements:

$$
B=\{-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,-\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\operatorname{cos}⁡x\}
$$

Consequently, $|B|=4,$ which is finite.

- The set $C$ is infinite. Listing the first few elements of our set, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{(0)}(x) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x \\ {h}^{(1)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)=\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ {h}^{(2)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)=2{sec}^{3}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x \\ ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we can write our set as follows:

$$
C=\{\operatorname{sec}⁡x,\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x,2{sec}^{3}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x,…\}
$$

Consequently, $C$ is infinite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$A$ and $C$ only."

q-108044.name: Question 13
q-108044.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1.$

II. $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3.$

III. If $v$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2,$ then $3v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda =-6.$
q-108044.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =1v.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $Av=v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =1$ (but not $-1$).

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =-3\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-3v.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $Av=-3v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-3.$

- Statement III is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(3v)=3Av=3(-2v)=-2(3v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(3v)=-2(3v),$ and $3v\ne 0,$ this implies that $3v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-2$ (but not $-6$).

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

q-14614.problem: The equation of a curve is $xy+{x}^{2}=1.$ The normal line at the point $(1,\,0)$ intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
q-14614.worked_solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(1,\,0).$   Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{′},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy+{x}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) & =0 \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y+2x & =0 \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-(2x+y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2x+y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,0)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(1,\,0)} \\  & ={(-\frac{2x+y}{x})}_{(1,\,0)} \\  & =-\frac{2\cdot 1+0}{1} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is ${m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{-2}=\frac{1}{2}.$ We can write the equation of the normal at the point $(1,\,0)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & ={m}^{′}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-0) & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}(0-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,-\frac{1}{2}).$

q-42956.problem:
Find the determinant of the matrix 
$K=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ -2 & \,-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 8 & 1\end{aligned}].$
q-42956.worked_solution:
Notice that the $4$th column contains three zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $4$th column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(K) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ -2 & \,-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 8 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{4+4}|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 4 \\ -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 4 \\ -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the $3$rd column of the $3\times 3$ determinant contains two zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $3$rd column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(K) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 4 \\ -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =4\cdot (-1)^{1+3}|\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(2-0) \\  & =4\cdot 2 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$
